title: A common-wealth of women a play : as it is acted at the Theatre Royal, by Their Majesties servants / by Mr. D'Urfey.
author: D'Urfey, Thomas, 1653-1723.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: MY Love!

speeches.speaker: Amint.
prose: I hope I am.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose:
Most certain; so punctual, and so fair, it must
be she!

speeches.speaker: Amin.
prose:
Punctual, you have reason to own me, for if you knew the
Difficulty I have undergone, to get out to you.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose:
I can guess at it, and am too sensible of the Villany of that
French-firework, thy Damn'd Guardian, not to know the Difficulty.
But 'prithee tell me, what pretty Stratagem did Love instruct thee
with, to make me thus happy?

speeches.speaker: Amin.
prose:
After Dinner, 'tis always his Custom to call for Tea, in
which I cunningly infus'd a Dram or two of Opium, which made its
Operation instantly; for after sneezing two or three times, and according
to his usual manner, fetching a Rhumatick Cough from the
bottom of his Lungs, which I always pray heartily may choak him.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose:
And so do I too, Faith. I hope our prayers will be heard
one Day.

speeches.speaker: Amin.
prose:
He fell fast asleep, and by that means gave me Opportunity
to meet an ungrateful Creature here, that is more ready to laugh at
me for my Weakness, than reward me for my Love.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose:
What a barbarous thought is that! Deny it, and make me
amends, or I swear I will kiss thee into an Extasie.

speeches.speaker: Amint.
prose:
Oh! I am fond and foolish: All my Actions shew Woman,
silly Woman, and must confess, deserve it.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose:
Prithee, no more of this, it wrongs my Love. And since we
have leasure to talk an Hour, make me so happy to hear the remainder
of thy Story; the story of thy Father, and the manner of thy
bringing hither to England, under the Tuition of that Villain, that
Cursed Pirate La Mure: You have often begun it, but we have bin
still interrupted.

speeches.speaker: Amint.
prose:
'Tis a sad Tale; but I can deny you nothing: If you remember
then, I told you that Don Sebastian was my Father. A generous
Portuguise; of Noble House, and Nature; and Governour of
several large Plantations in the Happy Islands; his Industry and Care
made him so rich, that he might vie with Princes; so stor'd he was
with Friends and Gifts of Fortune! But many years he had not thus
continued, when Hell contriving how to blast our Joys; drove on our
Shore a number of French Pyrates; of which La Mure was the most
Villainous, and being Captain of the rest, and well stor'd with Ammunition,
enter'd upon our Fortress, ruin'd our Plantations; and
chas'd the Peaceful Industrious Portugals, like Flocks of Sheep upon
the barren Mountains.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Inhumane Villains!

speeches.speaker: Amin.
prose:
My Father, in this distress, willing to save his Treasure, with
the help of my Brother, and a Party of Negro Slaves, secretly Convey'd
his Plate, Money, and Jewels into a small Vessel, and put to Sea,
with design-to return, when they were gone, and comfort us with
his Fortune and Policy.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: The Design was prudent, whatever the Event was.

speeches.speaker: Amin.
prose:
Oh it was fatal! For this Curst La Mure having Intelligence
by his Spies of my Fathers escape, and not knowing how to pursue
him, turn'd his rage upon my poor Mother, my Sister, and my self.
And having Laden his Ship with the Spoils and Riches of our Island,
carried us with him, and the put to Sea.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Where will this end?

speeches.speaker: Amin.
prose:
You shall know instantly. And the greatest Barbarity that
ever Villain acted: For sailing thence a few Leagues, and resolving
to be revenged on us, for the loss of my Father's Treasure, he leaves
my sighing Mother and a little Sister alone and comfortless upon a
wild and barren Island.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Damn'd Hellish Dog!

speeches.speaker: Amin.
prose:
And since that hour, I never heard of 'em. As to my self, (tho'
an Infant,) it pleas'd his Devil-ship to like my face. And therefore
brought me, (with my Nurse, who has since told me this Story;)
with him to London; where I have liv'd a melancholly and hated




Life ever since: And now am hourly plagu'd with the intollerable
Harangues of his Nauseous Love, and Impertinent Follies. Oh Marine!

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Why sighs, my dearest?

speeches.speaker: Amin.
prose: What shall I do?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: I'le tell thee, and charge thee by thy Love,
Nay, by thy Soul, and its divinest Virtue,
To perform my Injunction.

speeches.speaker: Amin.
prose: Can I with Honour do it?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Yes, else I would nor propose it.

speeches.speaker: Amin.
prose:
Speak then, nay quickly, for I fear he'll wake e're I get
back agen.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: This coming night,
When the Tell-tale Clock has told its midnight story,
And sleep Charms all but Libertines and Lovers,
Steal from his House, and fall into my Arms;
I have a Ship lies ready in the Port,
Laden and fit to sail, the wind stands fair too,
In her I'le place my Love, and free her from
The hated bondage of her Cursed Jaylor.

speeches.speaker: Amin.
prose: Oh! I shall ne're endure the Sea agen.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose:
Rather endure a Storm in all its frights and dangers, than
live to be enslav'd to Villany.

speeches.speaker: Amin.
verse: But if you shou'd forsake me! Oh misery!
And leave me helpless on some blasted Countrey,
As he once did my Mother!

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose:
Yet more doubts: by all that's good, you wrong me; prithee
no more of it. Come, your Promise?

speeches.speaker: Amin.
prose: I do: I must.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: At twelve.

speeches.speaker: Amin.
prose: Exactly.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Till then farewell. Heaven and its Angels guard thee.

speeches.speaker: Amin.
prose: Oh Love! thou mak'st us do we know not what.

speeches.speaker: Bolds.
prose:
Nay prithee Lieutenant, get off further; Life, I am affraid
the Fellow is kill'd.

speeches.speaker: D. Pier.
prose:
Kill'd! Hang him; no Sword can hurt him;
His Soul and all his Spirits are shrunk so low into his heels. 'Tis
impossible any wound given him should be Mortal. A Slave, to abuse
our noble Admiral. By this Hilt, if thou hadst not stood in my way,
I would have cut the Rogue into Stakes, and have eaten him up for
my Breakfast.

speeches.speaker: Marin.
prose: How now, Lieutenant, what's the matter?

speeches.speaker: D. Pier.
prose:
Captain, your Humble Servant. I Plague on't, I know not,
a damn'd huffing fellow yonder, a Rebel, Whiggy Buffle head—I know
not what to make of him, not I—had the Impudence, to my Face, to
affront our great Master the Admiral.

speeches.speaker: Marin.
prose: And thou hast kill'd him, I warrant.

speeches.speaker: D. Pier.
prose:
Clapt him through the Guts—Ham-string'd him; broke
out six or seven of his Teeth with the Pummel of my Sword, or so:
But I'le be pox'd, if he does not live to be hang'd, for all this.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose:
Prithee, do not thou tempt thy Fate, and live to be hang'd
instead of him: Our City Juries will shew thee but little favour or
affection, if thou once com'st into their Clutches.

speeches.speaker: D. Pier.
prose:
Consume 'em: I'le sooner make my self Immortal, with
a pennyworth of Rats-bane, than stand to the Courtesie of such a Cry
of Blood-hounds. But prithee, Captain, when shall we to Sea agen? Pox
o', this Dirty part of the World, a Man only fowls his Linnen
here, and draws Air amongst a rout of Rebels—I am clearly for
the Watry Element: And had rather Converse with Dolphins, Whales,
and Porpices, than our Natives: Why, they are honest Creatures,
and better Company.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose:
They are so i'faith: And thou shalt be with them suddenly.
For I have some urgent business will call me aboard within these
few hours. And to morrow, if the Wind sit fare, adieu old England.

speeches.speaker: D. Pier.
prose:
By the green Neptune, I am glad on't: A Brummingham
Son of a Whore, affront the Noble Admiral! Nay, 'tis well they
scour'd, we should have made a separation between some of their
Souls and Bodies else before this time, hah, Master!

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: What, has my Master bin in the Skirmish too?

speeches.speaker: D. Pier.
prose:
Yes Faith, the old Lad was all hands aloft with 'em.
I saw him clap one of 'em thro' the Shoulder, and throw a couple
more into the Cellar; that I saw him do.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Why, well said old Sea-mark.

speeches.speaker: Bolds.
prose:
Me! Why, how now, d'ee doubt me? Give me but a good
Cause, and a good Sword, and if I flinch, hang me on the Top-Mast-head,
or flea me, and make Ship-Buckets of my Hide. What, I
have not had so many Towels drawn through me for nothing, sure!

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose:
Ha, ha, ha. But hark you, Lieutenant, a word with thee; I
must require thy assistance in a business to night.

speeches.speaker: D. Pier.
prose:
Require—Command, dear Captain! Pox of requirings and
requests—your Ear—is there a Man or a Woman in the Case?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose:
A Woman, Du Piere! an Angel-Woman! a Fortune too,
and Young as the Rose-bud—Beautiful as the Blushing Morning; and
as willing as my self.

speeches.speaker: D. Pier.
prose:
Good. Well, must we scale for her, or steal her Cunningly?
Must we mount the Counterscarp like Men of Mettle; or squeeze
our selves, like Cats, into the Cellar Window?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Neither; she will meet us half way.

speeches.speaker: D. Pier.
prose:
Gad, a Gentlewoman I warrant her: Is there no one else
but her to take care of?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose:
Why, Faith yes, there may a Man come into her rescue,
which if it happen, I must enjoyn thee to—

speeches.speaker: D. Pier.
prose: Cut his Throat—Humh.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose:
No, no: onely oppose him, whilst I get off with my fair
Prize.

speeches.speaker: D. Pier.
Mar.
prose:
But what shall we do for a third Man, in case of Danger?
who, amongst the Ships Crew, can we trust in such a business?

speeches.speaker: D. Pier.
prose:
Why, Old Tarr there, against the World: There was not
such another for a Wench, since Noah's Flood.

speeches.speaker: Bolds.
prose:
Captain, if you dare trust me in your Affair, they shall saw
off my Beard with a Back-Sword, e're I leave you: Tho' I care not
this for the Woman—for my part, I am past these things.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose:
Well, well, my good Friend, I will be oblig'd to thee. Go
then instantly and prepare the Barge, and meet me at Eleven, here
at the Corner of the Piazza.

speeches.speaker: D. Pier.
prose:
The Wind favours our Design rarely too; besides, we
shall have more Company, for there are three or four young Blades,
Acquaintance of mine, that it seems are married to ill Wives, and
to avoid 'em, design to take a Ramble, and go Reformades with us;
for I told 'em it could not be long before we should put to Sea; and since
it happens thus opportunely—I'le send instantly to give 'em notice.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose:
Do—if they are of the Town-breed, they may prove very
good Diversion for us.

speeches.speaker: D. Pier.
prose:
The best in the World, Faith, I know 'em to a Hair—They
supt to night at the Rose, and I believe are there still, for they are
no Starters, to my knowledge—I'le step into your Lodging, since 'tis
so near hand, and write a Letter to 'em to be ready.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose:
I'le go with thee, and prepare all things for our Adventure—Ah,
Lieutenant! This Fortune-stealing is a blessed business, is it not?

speeches.speaker: D. Pier.
prose:
Ah, if she were but old, tough, and stanch! Pox on't, I
hate your young Weehees, Skitish Colts—they are so hard mouth'd,
there's no dealing with 'em.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: I hope to see thee fitted one day: Come, Let's away,—

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose: ARe we all agreed then?

speeches.speaker: Frug. Haz.
prose: All, all! most Constantly.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose:
Let's hear the Oath once more. Come, Frugal—my Merchant
Royal; thou shalt be Speaker. Silence.

speeches.speaker: Frug.
prose:
First we have sworn to take a Ramble to Sea for three years,
and during that Term, we have oblig'd our selves never to converse
with our Wives, kiss our Wives, nor remember our Wives.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose:
No, nor Children, but let them stay at home, keep Lent,
and chew the Cud.

speeches.speaker: Frug.
prose: And to this we all once more swear.

speeches.speaker: All.
prose: All, all.

speeches.speaker: Frug.
prose: Kiss the Book.

speeches.speaker: Haz.
prose:
But harkee, Gentlemen, now I have sworn this, 'tis fit I
should know the meaning on't—'Tis but just we declare some Reasons
why we leave our Wives,—hah?

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose: 'Tis so: Let one speak then, and the other two shall be Judges.

speeches.speaker: Haz.
prose: Do you begin then.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose:
With all my Heart: Why, first then, most Judicious Auditors,
the Reason why I desert my Matrimony is, because she grudges
me my Dress, and Garniture, and takes more care to Lace her own
Petticoat, than my Pantaloons. Besides, she knows that Dress and
Garniture, as I said before, are the only Comforts of my Life: I
should lead the life of a Dog, if it were not for my Feathers, my
Fiddles, and my Fineries: But I'le be reveng'd for her, for I have
prepar'd a Wardrobe, that shall outshine the Sun in the new World,
where we are going. And resolve to bid adien to my damn'd Dog
with a Bottle at home: What say you now? Have I not
Reason?

speeches.speaker: Frug.
prose: Reason! reason! great reason.

speeches.speaker: Haz.
prose: Reason! reason! great reason.

speeches.speaker: Haz.
prose: Come, now Merchant—now, let's here thine?

speeches.speaker: Frug.
prose:
Mine! nay, if I have not Reason, the Devil's in't! Mine!
why, look ye, In the first place, Gentlemen, you must know that I am
a Cuckold.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose: Very good.

speeches.speaker: Frug.
prose:
My Wife is an eternal Scold, and had two By-blows before
I marry'd her.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose:
Hem! Let's have no more on't; Tace! thou hast very Substantial
Reason, Faith.

speeches.speaker: Haz.
prose: Most Powerful! there's great strength of Reason in't.

speeches.speaker: Frug.
prose:
I think so. Besides, she was lavish and extravagant, and continually
rail'd at my Usury, and honest turning the penny: but to
be reveng'd on her, I cunningly broke lately, have put all my Plate,
Money, and Jewels into two Chests, and intend to seek some other
Countrey; where I will live, grow rich, and plant a Colony. Now
your approbations, Gentlemen? Have I not Reason?

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose:
Ay; the Deme take me, if thou hast not. But come Sharper,
now for thee. What occasion hadst thou to leave thy Wife?

speeches.speaker: Haz.
prose: Oh! occcasion enough, Faith.

speeches.speaker: Frug.
prose: What, prithee?

speeches.speaker: Haz.
prose: Because I could not keep her.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose: Pithy and short.

speeches.speaker: Frug.
prose: A very solid Reason in troth, and must pass muster.

speeches.speaker: Haz.
prose:
Besides, I have had an Antipathy to Woman-kind, ever
since I saw one of 'em unscrue her Nose one night—Oh, that Nose!
that Nose has stuck in my Stomach plaguily.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose:
Hell. I see we are all fixt, and of one mind: And resolve
to forget and despise that Vexatious and Impertinent Sex. For my
own part, I hate a Woman heartily.

speeches.speaker: Haz.
prose: And I.

speeches.speaker: Frug.
prose: And all things with flat. Bottoms I abominate.

speeches.speaker: Drawer.
prose:
Sir, here's a Letter just now left at our House, directed
to you.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose: News, news, my Lads! rare news!

speeches.speaker: Haz.
prose: What, prithee?

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose:
The Captain's just a going; the Ship is fall'n down, and
the Barge given order for: here's a Letter from the Lieutenant,
that says, they'l be gone by four a Clock this morning. I'le e'en go
instantly and get ready my Money and Wardrobe: And then adieu
dear Dog with a Bottle, as I said before.

speeches.speaker: Frug.
prose: And I my Chests of Plate and Jewels.

speeches.speaker: Haz.
prose:
And I my Cat, and my Bale of Dice: For that's all my
Cargo.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose: Come away, Boys; make haste, we shall lose the wind else.

speeches.speaker: Frug.
prose: I'le be ready in a moment.

speeches.speaker: Haz.
prose:
If I can but draw 'em in to play in the new World, where
we are a going—I am made for ever. Well, Fortune for me, there
lyes all my hopes.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: DOst thou see that Light in the Window there?

speeches.speaker: D. Pier.
prose:
Yes, I thank my Fortune, I have been acquainted
with such Stars before now: And on these Occasions two: But I had rather
that Meteor were extinguisht for all that, Captain, left we
should be seen.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: 'Tis past twelve, and few people pass this way.

speeches.speaker: D. Pier.
prose:
I fancy your Fortune-stealer to be very like your Venison-stealer,
that thinks himself oblig'd to the Moon, till he has got
his Game, but afterwards wishes her in a dark-Lanthorn, for fear
it should be taken from him.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose:
Master, be sure you scout diligently, and tell us if any
one comes.

speeches.speaker: Bolds.
prose:
Go too, go too, mind your Business, and make haste;
'tis well there's Money in the Case. Before I would stand quaking
here for a squab-sucking Rabbit; that's hardly worth the skinning,
I'd as soon stand Sentinel upon one of the Moles at Argier, tho' I
were sure of neither Pay, nor Provender.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Hark! What noise was that? Didst hear no noise?

speeches.speaker: D. Pier.
prose:
Some body at prayers, I think: Pox on't, we shall have ill
luck.

speeches.speaker: Bolds.
prose:
'Tis some dreaming Phanatick or other is singing of Psalms
in's sleep.

speeches.speaker: D. Pier.
prose:
Come, Captain, prithee give the Sign. I long to have the
Treasure in our Custody: That if any resistance happens, we may
fight for something.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose:
This must be the Door. Harkee, Lieutenant, prithee look
to that corner of the Street—I think I hear the Constable and
Watch.

speeches.speaker: D. Pier.
prose:
No. Rot 'em, they are making themselves drunk with Brandy.
They'l ne'er mind us. Come, come, the sign, the sign.

speeches.speaker: Amin.
prose: Who's there?

speeches.speaker: D. Pier.
prose: What's that there in white?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Hush, it must be she.

speeches.speaker: D. Pier.
prose:
In her Smock, I hope: To make a quicker dispatch of
the Business.

speeches.speaker: Amint.
prose: Who's there?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: 'Tis I.

speeches.speaker: Amin.
prose: Are you alone? What's that yonder?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Two worthy Friends, that I've intrusted to assist me.

speeches.speaker: Amin.
prose:
Oh my my Love: How shall I get to thee? For this jealous
Wretch has taken the Key of the Street door into his Chamber.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Leap into my Arms, I can bear thy weight with ease.

speeches.speaker: Bolds.
prose:
'Sbud, would I had her weight in Tobacco or Pepper.
Why, what a bustle's here with a green Artichoak?

speeches.speaker: Amin.
prose:
No—I must venture to get it from thence: In the mean
time, catch this Casket; keep it diligently; for 'tis worth your Care:
whil'st I go and try my Fortune.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose:
Make haste, my Dearest: For I am impatient, till I have
thee in my Arms. Lieutenant!

speeches.speaker: D. Pier.
prose: How now? What has Heav'n sent us?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose:
There's something in this Casket, Lieutenant, that will pay
for our trouble.

speeches.speaker: D. Pier
prose:
Why, merry be her Heart: I like a Wench that pays well
for her Man, before she has him: And of all Mistresses, your giving
Mistress ought most to be admir'd.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Heark, what's that?

speeches.speaker: D. Pier.
prose:
Mischief! I'le lay my Life: The Truce is broken, and
War will ensue. Tarr, hawl up thy Main Sheet, there's a Storm a
coming.

speeches.speaker: Amin.
prose: Oh, undone, undone! ruin'd for ever!

speeches.speaker: D. Pier.
prose: I thought so.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose:
What's the matter, Sweet! Fear nothing. Thou art safe as
in a Castle here.

speeches.speaker: Amin.
prose:
Eagerly reaching the Key out of the Window, my Sleeve
hitcht in the great Looking-glass, pull'd it after me, and broke it in
pieces: Which has, I am sure, alarm'd the House. Hark—I hear
'em coming.

speeches.speaker: D. Pier.
prose:
Well, well, and let 'em come. Captain, retreat you off
with your Lady. Tarr, Come hither, and fix thy foot to mine: By
this Hilt, if they come on, we'll mawle 'em.

speeches.speaker: Bolds.
prose:
Is there any Plunder to be got, Boy? This scouring for nothing,
is such cold Work—

speeches.speaker: La Mur.
prose:
O Diable! Rascal! Robera Teefe! V'ere are yee? Vat
hoa! Iacka, Petra, Tobee! Vere are ye all, Sons of Whore? I am
robbe: Oh Jernee! Mondieu. Here de are! fall on.

speeches.speaker: D. Pier.
prose:
Harkee, Diable! Rascale! Teefe! or what do you call your




self? Get you gon, or I shall so pink your Guts, d'ee hear?

speeches.speaker: La Mur.
prose: Morbleu, Villain! pinka my Guts. Courage.

speeches.speaker: D. Pier.
prose: Nay, if you will be paunch'd, have at your French paunch.

speeches.speaker: Bourch.
prose: What, hoa, Watch! Watch! Thieves, Thieves, murder.

speeches.speaker: Bolds.
prose: Sirrah, I'le spoil your Cackling presently.

speeches.speaker: Const.
prose: Stand, who goes there?

speeches.speaker: D. Pier.
prose:
Oh, Mr. Constable, you are come opportunely: Here are
a Company of disguis'd Turks, wou'd have Committed a rape upon
a Lady just now; if it had not bin for this Gentleman, and my self.

speeches.speaker: Const.
prose: How, Turks in my Territories!

speeches.speaker: D. Pier.
prose: Notorious ones. They are all hous'd within there.

speeches.speaker: Const.
prose:
Do I represent the Kings Person, and suffer Mahomet under
my Nose, hah?

speeches.speaker: La Mur.
prose: Monsieur Constable, Monsieur Constable!

speeches.speaker: D. Pier.
prose:
Seize, Seize him, Mr. Constable. He is a Mufti; and came
over from St. Omers, with Doctor what d'ee call him?

speeches.speaker: Const.
prose: A Mufti! down with him, down with him, I say.

speeches.speaker: La Mur.
prose:
Why, Monsieur Constable, vat you do? Is de Teevil
in you?

speeches.speaker: Watch.
prose: Search the House, search the House—

speeches.speaker: Du Pier.
prose:
Come
^arr, let's put off now: And go aboard immediately:
I think the Coast is clear—

speeches.speaker: Ro'ds.
prose:
LAy her aloof: the Sea grows Boistrous: How it spits
against the Clouds! how it Capers! And how the
Thunder-thumping Element frights it back—There are Devils dancing
Air, I think; I saw a Dolphin just now hang in the Horns of
the Moon—shot from a Wave! Hey, how she kicks! how she yerks!
Down with the Main Mast there, lay her at Hull. Furle up her Linnens,
and let her ride it out.

speeches.speaker: 1. Sail.
prose:
She'll never brook it, Master: She's so deep Laden, that
she'll bulge.

speeches.speaker: 2. Sail.
prose:
We have discover'd the Land, Sir; pray let's make in,
she's so drunk, she may chance to cast up her Lading.

speeches.speaker: 1 Sail.
prose: Stand in, Stand in. We are all lost else.

speeches.speaker: Bolds.
prose:
Steer her a Starboard there. What, hoa! call up the Boatswain.
Holloa—below there!

speeches.speaker: Boats.
prose:
What says my Master? what shall we do? We must cast up
all her Lading: She will not swim an hour else.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose:
What comfort, Master? I never saw, since I've known the Sea,
so rude a Tempest! In what condition are we?

speeches.speaker: Bolds.
prose:
Dangerous enough, Sir. We have sprung five Leaks; and
no little ones; Besides, her Ribs are open: and Rudder almost spent:
But come, have good Courage. Death comes out once, and let him
come in all his fury.

speeches.speaker: Boats.
prose: The Storm is so lowd, we cannot hear one another.

speeches.speaker: D. Pier.
prose: What's the Coast.

speeches.speaker: Boats.
prose: We know not yet. Let's bear in with all the Sail we can.

speeches.speaker: Surg.
prose:
Master, see what a Thunder-clap is coming: Oh Lord! how
dreadful it looks.

speeches.speaker: D. Pier.
prose:
Ye fearful Rogue. Sirrah, thou hast bin praying, I see it in
thy Face; thou hast bin mumbling, when we are splitting. You Slave,
is this a time to discourage your Friends with your Cold Ejaculations:
Sirrah—let me but see thee look Religiously agen, and I'le flea thee,
as I would an Eele.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Is't not possible to make in to the Land? 'Tis here before us.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose: Here, hard by, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Boldsp.
prose: Death is nearer, Gentlemen.

speeches.speaker: Frug.
prose: Oh, oh, oh.

speeches.speaker: D. Pier.
prose:
Why, there's another Rogue now with his Bagpipes:
Prithee, Dear Captain, give me leave to throw that Maudlin Fellow
over-board.

speeches.speaker: Haz.
prose: Come let's go in, and read.

speeches.speaker: Frug.
prose: Ay, come—

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose:
Let's hoist the Boat out, and go all at one Cast; the more
the merrier.

speeches.speaker: Bolds.
prose:
Hold, you are too hasty, Captain; d'ee long to be in the
Fish-market, before your time? hold her up there.

speeches.speaker: Amint.
prose: Oh miserable Fortune!

speeches.speaker: D. Pier.
prose: So! now we are like to have rare Musick?

speeches.speaker: Chapl.
prose: Mercy, mercy, what will become of us? Pray, Gentlemen—pray.

speeches.speaker: D. Pier.
prose:
Lookee! prithee, my Dear; no more words now, by this
Light—thou art the most unseasonable Rogue in a Storm.
Nay, prithee be gone.

speeches.speaker: Chapl.
prose: Pray, Gentlemen; pray, pray—

speeches.speaker: Amint.
prose:
Nothing but horrour sounding in my Ears: No promise
of rest to my poor frighted Soul! gentle Master, is there
no hopes?

speeches.speaker: Bolds.
prose: None, that I know! Dev'l, Clap this Woman under hatches.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Prithee speak mildly to her. Have patience, Sweet.

speeches.speaker: Bolds.
prose: Keep her thus, keep her thus.

speeches.speaker: Amint.
prose: Oh, that Wave will devour me! Oh—

speeches.speaker: Bolds.
prose:
Carry her down, Captain—or by these hands I'le
give no more Direction. We have ne're better Luck, when we
have such Stowage as these Trinckets with us. These sweet Sin-breeders;
how can Heaven smile on us—when such a Burthen of Iniquity—lyes
tumbling like a potion in the Ships belly.

speeches.speaker: Amint.
verse: What shall I do, my Heart and Senses fail me?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Come in with me. And try if thou canst sleep:
Thy pretty Heart wild-fears so long have rock'd;
Calm rest will steal upon it.

speeches.speaker: Amint.
verse: Oh Marine,
Remember, 'tis for you I meet these Dangers.
For you, expose my self to Seas and Horrors, and fears innumerable.

speeches.speaker: Marine.
prose: I know thou do'st.

And think too, I have treasur'd the Remembrance within me here,
fast lock'd up in my heart; and yet I doubt not but a Day will
come—To Crown our flourishing Loves, and make us happy.

speeches.speaker: Bolds.
prose: Throw out the Lading, it must all over-board.

speeches.speaker: Boats.
prose:
It clears to Sea ward, Master: Heave out there: Let's lighten
her! all the Meat and the Cakes. We are all gone else. That
we may find her Leaks, and hold her up.

speeches.speaker: Frug.
prose:
Must my goods over too? Kind, honest Master:
Why, here lies all my Money—the Money I have rak'd by




Usury, to buy new Lands and Mannors in new Countreys.—I have
been these 20 years a raising.

speeches.speaker: D. Pier.
prose: Over with it.

The Devils are got together by the Ears, who shall have it.—And
here they quarrel in the Clouds.

speeches.speaker: Frug.
prose: Oh, I am undone!

speeches.speaker: D. Pier.
prose: Hang ye, Mungrels, would you be only happy?

speeches.speaker: Frug.
prose: Save but one Chest of Plate!

speeches.speaker: D. Pier.
prose:
Away with it lustily, Sailers; it was some Pawn that he has
got unjustly, down with it low enough; and let Crabs breed in't.

speeches.speaker: Boldsp.
prose: Over with the Truncks too.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Take mine, and spare not.

speeches.speaker: Bolds.
prose: Nay, nay; all that has weight must go.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose:
Will you throw away my Lordship, that I sold, to buy me a
fine Wardrobe—For pity's sake, be favourable to my fine Wardrobe.

speeches.speaker: D. Pier.
prose:
Over with it—I love to see a Lordship sink. My Friend,
you left no Wood upon't, to buoy it up, you might have sav'd it else.

speeches.speaker: Haz.
prose:
For my part, I have nothing of weight, but my Prayer-Book:
And that, I am resolv'd, shall not burden the Ship. There 'tis.—

speeches.speaker: D. Pier.
prose: Why, well said!

speeches.speaker: Surg.
prose: Come, come, Lieutenant, you may lose too.

speeches.speaker: D. Pier.
prose:
Thou ly'st: I have nothing to lose, but my Maidenhead,
my Skin, my Cloaths, my Sword here, and my Self, two Crowns in my
Pocket, two pair of Cards, and three false Dice—I can swim like a
Fish, Rascal, nothing to hinder me.

speeches.speaker: Boats.
prose: In with her of all hands.

speeches.speaker: Bolds.
prose:
Come Captain, come Gentlemen: Ye must all help, my Life
now for the Land. 'Tis high, and very Rocky.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: However, let's attempt it.

speeches.speaker: Bolds.
prose: Then Cheer lustily, my Hearts, and away with her.

speeches.speaker: Sebast.
prose:
IT must be a Ship—I see it now; a tall Ship, she has
wrought lustily for her Deliverance! Heav'ns Mercy! what
a dismal Day has here been?

speeches.speaker: Nicus.
prose:
To still and quiet Minds that know no Miseries, it may seem




wretched; but with us 'tis ordinary. Heav'n has no Storm in store,
nor Earth no Terror, that can seem new to us.

speeches.speaker: Sebast.
verse: 'Tis true, my Son;
If Fortune were determin'd to be wanton,
And wou'd wipe out the story of Mens Miseries,
Yet we two, living still, should cross her purpose:
Canst thou see 'em? Do they live still?

speeches.speaker: Nicu.
prose: Yes: and make to Shore!

speeches.speaker: Sebast.
prose: Most miserable Men, I pity 'em.

speeches.speaker: Nicu.
prose: What Shouts of Joy they make?

speeches.speaker: Sebast.
verse: Alas! poor Wretches!
Had they but once Experience of this Island,
They'd turn their Shouts to Howlings.

speeches.speaker: Nicu.
verse: Nay, to Curses!
That ever they set Foot on this fad place.

speeches.speaker: Sebast.
verse: Sad indeed: where nothing is but Rocks and Barrenness;
Hunger and Cold—Here's no Vineyards
To cheer the Heart of Man: Nor Chrystal Rivers,
After his Labour, to refresh his Body;
If he be Feeble, nothing to restore him,
But Heav'nly Hopes: Nature, that made those Remedies,
Dares not come here, nor look on our Distresses,
For fear she turn Wild, like the place, and Barren.

speeches.speaker: Nicu.
verse: Then, Sir, the memory of what we were,
When we were seated in our blessed Homes,
Gives us a double Misery.

speeches.speaker: Sebast.
verse: Oh Curse on those French Pirates that displanted us,
And drove me from my Wife and pretty Children,
To live a wretched Life, upon this fatal Island.

speeches.speaker: Nicu.
prose:
They are living yet, I hope, Sir; such Goodness
Cannot perish.

speeches.speaker: Sebast.
verse: They may live—but never to me, my Son,
Never to me again—Look on't—What bear
Their Flagg-staves?

speeches.speaker: Nicu.
verse: The Arms of England.

speeches.speaker: Sebast.
verse:
They get to Shore apace. What's that which
Swims?

speeches.speaker: Nicu.
verse: A strong young Man! with a hansom
Woman hanging about his Neck.

speeches.speaker: Sebast.
verse: A Noble Fellow, I warrant him!
May this brave Charity, who e're thou art,
Be spoken in a place that may renown thee,
And not dye here.

speeches.speaker: Nicu.
verse: Their Boat it seems turn'd over,
And forc'd them to their Shifts, yet all are landed—
They are certainly Pyrates.

speeches.speaker: Sebast.
verse: Let 'em be what they will, they will not Rob us;
For none will take our Misery for Riches;
Come, Son, let us descend, and try their Pities;
If we get off, we have a little hopes;
If not, we shall but load this wretched Island
With the same Shaddows still that must grow shorter.

speeches.speaker: D. Pier.
prose: Wet come a Shore, my Hearts; we are safe arriv'd tho'.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose:
Thanks to Heavens Goodness! and no Man lost neither, but the
poor Chaplain.

speeches.speaker: D. Pier.
prose:
Ay—the poor Soul-Broker's gone, he was wash'd, with
a Wave, off the Quarter-Deck—I saw his Cassock and he fluttering between
Wind and Water, a great while—Well, Peace be with him,
he was too good for us.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse:
The Weather's turn'd more Courteous: and the Ship rides fair
too, and her Leaks in good plight:
How does my Dear? Alas, poor Heart!
How weak she is, and wet!

speeches.speaker: Amint.
verse: I am glad I escap'd with Life:
For which, Dear Captain, I am oblig'd to you:
Oh let the Heav'ns but bless me with a means
How to reward such Love, and I am happy.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: This Rosy kiss rewards me ten times o're,
And this ten thousand.

speeches.speaker: Amint.
verse: I cannot speak for Joy.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: My Dearest Life—Well, what cheer, my Lads?

speeches.speaker: D. Pier.
prose:
Faith! no great Cheer, Captain! a piece of Sous'd Bisket,
and half a hard Egg: For the Sea has taken order, being young and
strong, we shall not surfeit: For my own part, the Water has made a
mear Toste of me; I am sopt rarely: However, I'le Dance. till I am
dry: Come, Surgeon, out with your Glister-pipe, Sirrah, and strike a
Galliard.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose:
Why, what a brave day is here? And what fair Weather, after
so foul a Storm?

speeches.speaker: Frug.
prose:
Ay, if the Master had not been bewitch'd, he might have foreseen
this Weather, and have sav'd our Goods! Oh my dear Plate and
Jewels! Oh my dear Money! Vengeance on the Master.

speeches.speaker: Franv.
prose:
Ay, and twenty small Curses beside; I have lost my fine
Wardrobe; oh insupportable! the Ladies will hate me.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Oh never think on 'em: VVe have our Lives and Healths!

speeches.speaker: Haz.
prose:
For my part I've lost nothing, but my Pray'r Book: I sav'd
my other Cargo, my bale of Dice: therefore I am happy.

speeches.speaker: Frug.
prose:
Not think of 'em, Sir! I must and will think of 'em: And
that 'twas most maliciously done, to undo me

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose:
And me too: I lost all:
I had fifteen fair Suits: the worst of 'em Embroider'd; and now I ha'n't
so much as a Shirt left.

speeches.speaker: D. Pier.
prose: Ha, ha, ha, hast not, Faith?

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose:
No, by this Light; nor ragg of Cloaths neither, but these
poor things.

speeches.speaker: D. Pier.
prose:
Give me thy hand: I am glad on't with all my Heart. Is
thy Skin whole?

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose: Sir, you may spare your Raillery.

speeches.speaker: D. Pier.
prose:
Faith, I shannot! Harkee, wilt thou see a Dog- fish now rise in
one of thy brave Doublets? And tumble like a Tub, to make thee merry?
Or an Old Haddock rise with thy Beaver Hat on? A Mermaid in a
Wastcoat of your Worships; or a Dolphin with your Point Crevat?

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose:
You are merry, Sir; but if I take it thus—if I be foisted and
jeer'd out of my VVardrobe—

speeches.speaker: Frug.
prose: Nor I, neither.

speeches.speaker: Haz.
prose: Nor will I leave my Friends.

speeches.speaker: Frug.
prose:
Neither Master, nor Mate, nor none of you shall abuse me:
I say our Goods might ha' been sav'd; and I'le have satisfaction.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Nay, be not angry, Gentlemen.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose: Sir, we have reason: And some Friends I can make.

speeches.speaker: Bolds.
prose:
Why, you Scoundrels! was not what I did for the general Safety?
if you aim at me, I am not so tame—

speeches.speaker: Haz.
prose: No, nor we neither.

speeches.speaker: D. Pier.
prose:
Pray take my Counsel, Gallants: Fight not till the Surgeon
be well, d'ee hear? He's damnable Sea-sick yonder: and may spoil all:
Besides he has lost his Fiddle-stick—And the best Box of Boars-grease.
Nay—do not draw your Swords; for if you do.—

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose:
Who would you fight with, Gentlemen? Who has done you
wrong? For shame be better temper'd; no sooner come to give thanks
for our safeties, but we must raise new Civil Broils among us—Put up,
put up, for shame.—

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose: We have been wrong'd, Sir, and damnably too.

speeches.speaker: D. Pier.
prose:
Nay, lookee; if you will needs fight, and think to raise
new Riches by your Valours, come—have at you: I have little else
to do now: I have said my Prayers—You say you have lost, and make
your Loss your Quarrel, and grumble at my Captain here, and the Master:
two worthy Persons, indeed, too worthy for such Rescals—Come
you Wardrobe Gallant, come on: and you, Money Merchant, that
build on Golden Monuments in Potosi. Come, draw all your Swords, ye
say ye are miserable?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose:
Put up, Gentlemen, or, by this light, he'll swinge you damnably—I
see't in's Face.

speeches.speaker: D. Pier.
prose:
Captain stand by a little: And see how I'le correct 'em.
I'le make 'em ten times poorer—I will not leave 'em—for
look you, fighting is as nourshing to me, as eating: I was born
quarrelling.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Come, they'l Consider.

speeches.speaker: D. Pier.
prose:
I will not leave 'em skin to cover 'em: there's no joint
shall stand in's proper place. D'ee grumble when you are well, you
Rogues?

speeches.speaker: Frug.
prose:
A Devilish Fellow this Lieutenant. Gad he has quash'd me
already.

speeches.speaker: D. Pier.
prose: 'Scape drowning, and d'ee prate?

speeches.speaker: Amint.
prose:
Pray, Gentlemen, for my sake be quiet; let it become me
to make all Friends.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose:
We have so much breeding, not to deny a Lady any thing:
Come let's put up.

speeches.speaker: Frug.
prose:
Ay, ay: We were to blame, to draw before the Lady, that's
the truth on't.

speeches.speaker: Haz.
prose: This Passion, and too much Courage, is a damnable fault.

speeches.speaker: D. Pier.
prose:
'Tis well, 'tis very well: There's half a Bisket, break
it amongst you all, and thank my Bounty; that is Cloaths and Plate
too now. Come no more quarrels.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose:
Ha! in the name of wonder, what have we here?
Are they humane Creatures?

speeches.speaker: D. Pier.
prose: I have heard of Sea-Calves.

speeches.speaker: Amint.
prose: They are no shadows sure, they have legs and arms.

speeches.speaker: D. Pier.
prose: Ay, they hang but scurvily on though.

speeches.speaker: Surg.
prose: What Beards they have?

speeches.speaker: D. Pier.
prose:
They have sown Horse Tails to their Faces, to keep—'em
warm.

speeches.speaker: Amint.
prose:
How their Eyes are sunk, as if they had bin frighted;
sure they are wretched Men?

speeches.speaker: D. Pier.
prose:
There are Wardrobes for you: Look you, my Friend,
what do you think of these now for a Couple of Courtiers?

speeches.speaker: Bolds.
prose: They kneel, sure they would beg something.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose:
What are you? Speak, are you Substances, or wandring shadows,
that find no peace on Earth, till you reveal some secret?

speeches.speaker: Sebast.
prose:
We are Men as you are, onely our Miseries make us seem
Monsters; if ever pity dwelt in noble Hearts—

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Stand up, and speak boldly.

speeches.speaker: Nicus.
prose:
If you are Christians, and by that blessed Name bound to
^elieve us. Convey us from this Island.

speeches.speaker: D. Pier.
prose: Speak—what are you?

speeches.speaker: Sebast.
verse: Of honourable Birth; to tell you more,
VVere but to number up our own Calamities,
And make our Eyes wilde with perpetual weepings;
This many years, in this most wretched Island
VVe two have liv'd, the Scorn and Game of Fortune,
Bless your selves from it! noble Gentlemen!
The greatest plagues that Humane Nature suffers,
Are seated here: VVildness and VVants innumerable.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: How came you hither?

speeches.speaker: Sebast.
prose:
In a small Vessel: Driven hither by French Pyrates, to save
my VVealth from those insulting Robbers.

speeches.speaker: Amin.
prose: French Pyrates! Oh my heart!

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Is all the Island uninhabited?

speeches.speaker: Nicus.
prose:
Most desolate, neither Man nor Beast to comfort or sustain
us.

speeches.speaker: Sebast.
verse: No summer here to promise any thing,
Nor Autumn to make full the Reapers hand;
The Earth, obdurate to the Tears of Heav'n,
Let's nothing shoot or grow, but poisonous VVeeds:
No Rivers, nor no pleasant Groves: No Beasts.
All that were made for Man's use, flye this place.
Serpents, and ugly things, the shames of Nature.
Roots of malignant tastes, foul standing VVaters,
Sometimes we finde a fulsome Sea Root,
And that's a Delicate; a Rat sometimes,
And that we hunt, like Princes in their pleasure;
And if we take a Toad, we make a Banquet.

speeches.speaker: Frug.
prose:
Oh Lord! we shall be starv'd too! Mercy on us, eat a Toad!
did he say?

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose:
VVould I were at home agen with my dear Matrimony, I begin
to be weary of rambling.

speeches.speaker: Amint.
prose:
For Heaven's sake, let's aboard, I would discourse with
this Fellow; for my mind gives me, he can tell me something of
my Father?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: D'ee know no farther?

speeches.speaker: Nicusa.
verse: VVe have sometimes seen the shadow of a place
Inhabited: And heard the noise of Hunters.
And have attempted to find it as far as a River,
Deep, slow, and dangerous, fenc'd with high Rocks,
VVould give us leave; but not able to atchieve that hazard,
Return'd to our old miseries: And, Gentlemen,
If this sad story may deserve your pities—

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: You shall aboard with us; we will relieve you.

speeches.speaker: Sebast.
verse: VVe will not be unthankful for this Benefit;
No, Gentlemen, we'll pay for our deliverance.
Look you, that plough the Sea, for wealth and pleasure,
That out-run Day and Night with your Ambitions:
Look on those heaps, remove 'em, view 'em fully.

speeches.speaker: D. Pier.
prose: By Heaven, 'tis Gold and Jewels!

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose: How!

speeches.speaker: Frug.
prose: VVhat's that? Gold and Jewels!

speeches.speaker: Sebast.
prose: Be not too hasty, here lies another heap.

speeches.speaker: Bolds.
prose: And here another; all Gold! by this Light.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Stand farther off, you must not be your own Carvers.

speeches.speaker: Frug.
prose:
VVe have shares, and large ones—I'le have my Plate
and Money made good.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose: And I my VVard-robe.

speeches.speaker: Haz.
prose:
Ay, and we'll Carve our selves too. VVhat hoa! Fellow-Sailers,
stand to your freedoms: Gold, gold.

speeches.speaker: Sebast.
verse: Take heed, Gentlemen;
This Gold was the overthrow of my happiness.
For landing here with a party of Negro-Slaves,
That I commanded to assist me against the Pyrates:

This cursed Gold enticing 'em, they set upon me, and my Son here;
wounded us almost to Death.
And then their Civil Swords, who should be owners:
First in their rage, consum'd the Vessel that brought us,
And next themselves by heaps. Oh be you wise and careful.

speeches.speaker: Frug.
prose:
Tell not me of Care, Sir—holloa! All that will share with
us—assist us. I'le have all this.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose: And I this.

speeches.speaker: D. Pier.
prose: You shall be hang'd first: Captain, let's set in.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: This Damn'd Gold will undo us all.

speeches.speaker: Frug.
prose: My Losses must be made good.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose: And so must mine; or else this Sword shall right me.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Nay if you will be Dogs—

speeches.speaker: D. Pier.
verse: Let me come, Captain.
This Golden Age must have an Iron ending:
Have at the Bunch.

speeches.speaker: Amint.
prose:
Stay, dear Marine! Lieutenant, oh Heavens! what will become
of us?

speeches.speaker: Sebast.
prose:
Now Fortune favour us. Come Son, if we stay here, we
dye: Here rides their Ship. Whilst they are gone to the spoil—let
us make quick use, and get off.

speeches.speaker: Nicus.
prose: Away—Dear Father.

speeches.speaker: Sebast.
prose: This Gold was our overthrow.

speeches.speaker: Nicus.
prose: It may be now our happiness.

speeches.speaker: D. Pier.
prose:
You shall have Gold: Yes! I'le cram it into you—you
shall be your own Carvers, yes; I'le carve you, base greedy Rogues.
Captain, let's make an end of 'em.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose:
No—hang 'em, though they are Villains, yet they are our
Countrey-men: prithee Master get the Boat ready, and let's aboard.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose: Oh, I am hurt to Death.

speeches.speaker: Frug.
prose: And I—my Leg is almost cut off—Oh.

speeches.speaker: Surg.
prose:
Oh Captain, we are undone, we are undone; all miserable!
ruin'd—lost—the ship—the Ship.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: What of her?

speeches.speaker: Surg.
prose:
Oh she's under sail, and floating: See where she flies—see
to your shames, you Wretches, those poor starv'd things that shew'd
us Gold, have chous'd us.

speeches.speaker: D. Pier.
prose: We are snapt finely.

speeches.speaker: Boats.
prose:
They have cut her Cables, and got her out: The Tide too
has befriended them.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose:
Oh damn'd misfortune! why, where were all the Saylers that
kept her?

speeches.speaker: Bolds.
prose:
Here in the mutiny, to take up Money, with a Pox to 'em:
And left no Creature; left the Boat a shore too. Oh this Gold!
This damn'd bewitching Gold.

speeches.speaker: Frug.
prose: Oh we shall be starv'd, we shall be starv'd.

speeches.speaker: Haz.
prose: Come back, good Men; come back, good old Men—

speeches.speaker: Frug.
prose: Come back, good honest Men.

speeches.speaker: D. Pier.
prose:
Come back, good Men, come back: Yes, 'tis very likely
they will! D'ee look like Dogs now? Are your mighty Courages
abated?

speeches.speaker: Amint.
prose: This is the worst of miseries: Oh what shall we do?

speeches.speaker: D. Pier.
prose:
Retire, Sir, and comfort her, and let us make the best
use of our Misfortune: I'le but vex these Rascals a little, and come
to you straight—

speeches.speaker: Frug.
prose: Oh I am hurt and hungry, hurt and hungry, very hungry.

speeches.speaker: D. Pier.
prose:
Here's a pestle of a Portigue, Sir. 'Tis excellent meat,
with soure Sawce: And here's two Chains, you may suppose 'em
Sawsages: Then there wants Mustard; but the Surgeon there will
supply that presently with Salves.

speeches.speaker: Surg.
prose:
My Salves, and all my Instruments are lost, and I am hurt
and starv'd.

speeches.speaker: D. Pier.
prose:
Starv'd! what in a Land that flows with Milk and Honey!




a second Canaan! Come, Faith, let's go all to supper.

speeches.speaker: Omnes.
prose: Ay, where's the meat?

speeches.speaker: D. Pier.
prose: Where's the meat? VVhy, what a Veal voice is there?

speeches.speaker: Frug.
prose: Veal—gad would we had it.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose:
Ay, or Mutton either: tho' 'twere of a rotten Sheep that
dy'd in a Ditch.

speeches.speaker: D. Pier.
prose:
Now would I cut your throats ye Dogs; but that I
won't do you such a Courtesie to keep you from the Benefit of
starving; which will be, and suddenly; unless you can eat Mud, and
fancy 'tis Custard; to which excellent repast, I leave ye: Your
first Couse is serv'd up. Expect the second hereafter—

speeches.speaker: Frug.
prose: Ah, Pox o' these Jewels.

speeches.speaker: Fran. Haz.
prose: Oh this Cursed Gold.—

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: NO Comfort yet, nor hopes of a relief,
No welcome Plant, or wholsome Fruit to help us,
Against oppressing Famine: Oh Heaven!
To what Fate do our Cruel Stars reserve us!
How does my Dear, art thou not faint and weak?

speeches.speaker: Amint.
prose: Not much; your Company is still a Cordial to me.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: You good Angels, that are ingag'd, when our Ability
Fails, to reward Virtue, look on this Lady;
For me, tho' Famine gripes my Croaking Entrai's,
Yet when I kiss these lips, methinks
I am at a Banquet; a refreshing Banquet.
Speak, my Dearest life, art thou not hungry?

speeches.speaker: Amint.
prose: Indeed, I could eat to keep you company.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Blush, unkind Nature! Canst thou supply a Drunkard?
And with a prodigal hand give choice of VVines,
Till he disgorge thy Blessings? Or a Glutton,
That robs the Element, to sooth his Pallat;
And onely Eats to beget Appetite,
Not to be satisfy'd? And suffer here
A Virgin, which the Saints wou'd make their Guest,
To pine for hunger.
Hah, if my Sense
Deceive me not, these sounds take Being
From the breath of Men: Confirm me, dear Aminta.
This way the gentle Wind convey's it to us;
Hear you nothing?

speeches.speaker: Amint.
verse: Yes, plainly; it seems the Hunters Musick.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Still 'tis louder: And I remember the two Portugals
Inform'd us, they had often heard such sounds;
But ne're could touch the Shore from whence they came.

speeches.speaker: Amint.
verse: Nor is it to be hop'd we shall: This envious
Torrent's cruelly interpos'd to hinder us, and we
Have no Vessel that may transport us:
Nor has Nature given us Wings to flye.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Better try all hazards,
Than perish here remediless.
To serve my sweet Aminta,
These Arms shall be my Oars, with which I'le swim,
And my Zeal, to save thy precious Innocence,
Like wings shall bear me up spite of these horrid waves.

speeches.speaker: Amint.
verse: Will you then leave me?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: But for a moment, Sweet: And believe,
Tho' pleasure met me in most ravishing Form;
And happiness courted me to entertain her,
I would not eat, nor sleep, till I return'd;
And Crown'd thee with my Fortune.

speeches.speaker: Amint.
verse: Oh but your Absence, and my Fears, what mischief
May happen to you in that Fatal place,
Will certainly distract me.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Suppose it but a Dream, and try to sleep.
Think you have sent me for discovery
Of some most fortunate Continent, yet unknown;
Which you are to be Queen of.
And all ye Powers, that Value Lovers prayers,
Or Cherish true affection, guard my Love
In your protection, let her cease to mourn,
Nor sigh, or shed a Tear till my return.

prose:
A SONG between two Amazons.



LIberty's the Soul of Living,
Every hour new Ioys receiving;
No sharp Pangs our hearts are grieving,
Liberty's the Soul of Living.


2.
Here are no false Men pursuing
Youth or Beauty to its Ruine
Murmuring sighs, like Turtles Cooing;
Nor the bitter Sweets of Wooing.
Liberty's the Soul of Living,
Liberty's the Soul of Living.





3.
In soft dreams our Souls are wasted,
All our solid Ioys are blasted.
Sweet Diana, e're I'm past it,
Change thy Law, and let me taste it.


4.
But how vain are Hopes or Sorrows,
Pensive Nights, or sighing Morrows
Love's a Prey, not destin'd for us.
All our Quivers want their Arrows.
There's no Liberty like Loving,
There's no Liberty like Loving.


Chorus of Both.
Then since, we are doom'd to be Chaste;
And loving is counted a Crime,
We'll to our new Pleasures make haste.
Sing, Revel, and laugh out our Time,
And do what we can,
Not to think of a Man,
But make the best use of our Prime.

speeches.speaker: Rosel.
verse: They that say Women are not fit to Govern,
Betray their weakness, and their want of Knowledge:
For what Perfection is there in the Male,
That is not in the Female: Grant, their Composure stronger,
Their Bodies Courser, and more fit for Wars,
Which some of us, do haply contradict:
I cannot yet Conceive, why this shou'd bind us
To be their Slaves; our Souls are Male as theirs;
And that we have hitherto forborn t'assume,
And mannage Thrones: I say, altho' we have not
Challeng'd a Soveraignty in Arts and Arms;
And writ our selves Imperial, hath bin
Mens Tyranny, and our Modesty—not defects,
Or want of Judgment: Blest be then the hour
That threw me on this Shore, inhabited by Warlike Women,
That keep men in Subjection: And by them, chosen to rule:
Where, since I lost Sebastian, and Nicusa;
My Husband, and dear Son, by those French Pyrates;
All others of their Sex have met my hate.

speeches.speaker: Clar.
verse: And shall they still do so?

speeches.speaker: Rosel.
verse: For ever, Girl!
Thou darling of my life: my Dear Clarinda,
I say for ever.

speeches.speaker: Hip.
prose:
And must I always dream, and dream then, and to no purpose—by
this light I will have a Husband, or she shall never live
a good day.

speeches.speaker: Ariad.
prose: Nay, the Protectress is too severe, that's the truth on't.

speeches.speaker: Iuliet.
prose:
Because she's Old, she thinks every one has as little Occasion
for a Husband, as her self: But she's mistaken in me, I can assure
Her.

speeches.speaker: Clita.
prose: Ay, and in me too.

speeches.speaker: Rosel.
verse: And therefore more to confirm my Resolution,
That we may still keep out insulting Man,
I here appoint, when-e're I chance to dye,
That the succession fall on my Clarinda.

speeches.speaker: Clar.
verse: Madam, with humblest Duty,
I pay my thanks: but fear the Common-wealth
Will murmur at this positive Election;
She being always chosen to Govern here,
That's voted by the People, as you were—

speeches.speaker: Hip.
prose: Which Custome shall continue. We'll have no Arbitrary proceedings.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
prose:
No: nor will we have our Privileges impos'd upon, unless she
will give us Men.

speeches.speaker: Rosel.
prose: What's that you murmur about men?

speeches.speaker: Menal.
prose:
Men! Out upon 'em, I'le assure your Highness, our thoughts
are—

speeches.speaker: Iul.
prose: Of nothing else, if the truth were known.

speeches.speaker: Rosel.
verse: Once more I vote Clarinda my Successor:
And will in this Position be obey'd,
Or like a storm my Rage lets loose upon ye:

prose:
I give you leave to consider—Menalippe, Clita, follow me. You are
too young to ingage in private Factions: And therefore meet my
pitty—but for the rest—

Let them take heed, how they my Will debate,
Or act a Crime they may repent too late.

speeches.speaker: Hip.
verse: She behaves her self, as if she were Immortal,
Or as the Sun, or she had equal Influence,
And did oblige the World with mutual Blessings.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
prose:
If such Pride as this hold long, we are like to have a hopeful
Government.

speeches.speaker: Ariad.
prose:
Ay, and without Men too, to keep us Company,
And be Civil to us, I assure ye: my Dears, now we are alone, and
have liberty to speak our thoughts, In my Opinion, this usage of our
Protectress is not to be endur'd.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
prose:
Endur'd! by my Virginity, 'tis downright Tyranny: For I
confess, for my own part, I have no liking to this single solitary
Life; nor do I love hunting other Creatures so well, but I had as
lieve be hunted my self.

speeches.speaker: Hip.
prose: Nor I, by Venus.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
prose:
By Venus! by Diana, I hope you meant to swear, Hippolita?
she, you know, had the most Virtues.

speeches.speaker: Hip.
prose: It may be so: But I'm sure t'other had the most Wit.

speeches.speaker: Ariad.
prose:
Very fine: I wish you could influence the Protectress with
this Doctrine.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
prose:
Pox on her, nothing can influence an old Woman, but a
Iulip.

speeches.speaker: Ariad.
prose:
Oh, Eringo's, or an Ownce or two of Green Ginger,
would work admirable Effects.

speeches.speaker: Hip.
prose:
I know not what Consolation she may have, but if I have any
Comfort in this life, but when I sleep, I am a Whore.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
prose:
A Whore! Oh Venus! what a sweet charming luscious honey
word, has this raw Creature thrown away—A Whore! what the
Devil, would you be an Angel?

speeches.speaker: Hip.
prose: Would I were a VVhore upon a good account.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
prose:
Or I either: Oh little England's a sweet place for this purpose,
the VVhores have as much respect there as the Women of
Quality.

speeches.speaker: Ariad.
prose: And more than their Wives, I hear, a thousand times.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
prose:
But you were talking of Dreams, Sweet-heart: And last night
I had the sweetest sure, that ever woman had; for methought as I




was lying in my Cabine, a fine young brisk, well shap'd man, stole
softly to me all unbutton'd, and taking me in his Arms, kiss'd me,
on my Conscience, above twenty times.

speeches.speaker: Ariad.
prose: Deuce take you: You have made my mouth run with water.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
prose:
Lord! what a man is this, thought I, to do this to a Maid:
And so stretching out my Arms, thinking to Catch him fast—

speeches.speaker: Hip.
prose: You wak'd, and found nothing—

speeches.speaker: Iul.
prose: Even so: Therefore the Devil take all false Figures, I say.

speeches.speaker: Hip.
prose:
And so say I too: For my part I have wish'd the Statues in
the Garden had bin real, a thousand times.

speeches.speaker: Clar.
verse: Come, Ladies, are you not for hunting?
VVe dull our selves for want of Exercise.
There's not a guilded Hour adorns the day;
But smiling, greets us with some new adventure;
Away for shame, and clog not your clear bloods
VVith that perpetual Bane of Beauty, Idleness.

speeches.speaker: Hip.
prose: Madam, we wait on you: Who rouz'd the Stag?

speeches.speaker: Menal.
prose:
Clarinda, and in the instant,
Lodg'd a Steel-Headed Arrow in his Hanch,
VVith which he's fled.

speeches.speaker: Hip.
prose: Ha, what's this comes here?

speeches.speaker: Ariad.
prose: By all that's good, a man: shall I shoot him.

speeches.speaker: Clar.
prose: No, no: 'Tis a handsome Beast, sure.

speeches.speaker: Menal.
prose:
VVould we had more o' the Breed, really 'tis a very
Comely Creature.
Let's hear if it can speak?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: VVhat Heavenly place is this?
VVhere Beings more than humane keep their Residence?
Sure I have past the Baleful stygian Gulf?
And now touch on the blessed Shore: 'Tis so,
This is Elizium: And these the happy Spirits;
That here enjoy all pleasures.

speeches.speaker: Clita.
prose: He comes towards us! O Lord! won't it eat me?

speeches.speaker: Hip.
prose: Stand, or I'le shoot.

speeches.speaker: Clar.
prose: Hold—he makes no resistance.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Be not offended Goddesses, that I fall
Thus prostrate at your feet? Or, if not such,
But Nymphs of Diana's Train, that range these Groves;
Which you forbid to men: Vouchsafe to know,
That tho' I am a man, I am not sold
So far to Impudence, as to presume
To press upon your privacies for my self,
No, that I am an humble Suiter to you,
Is for a Virgin—Comes as near your selves
In all perfection, as what's mortal may
Resemble things Divine: O pity her,
And let your Charity free her from you Desart;
If Heavenly Charity can reach to Hell.
For sure that place comes near it: And where e're
This wretched frame of mine shall find a Being,
Eternally I shall pour Blessings on you.

speeches.speaker: Hip.
verse: By my Maden-head I cannot hurt him now:
Well, some of these mankind have strange influences.

speeches.speaker: Menal.
verse: Really, 'tis the finest thing that ever I saw in my life:
Wou'd he wou'd come and kiss me.

speeches.speaker: Clar.
prose: Cruel Hippolita, how could'st thou find in thy Heart to kill him?

speeches.speaker: Hip.
prose: Madam, if I had done it, I had but obey'd your Mother's Commands.

speeches.speaker: Clar.
verse: If she Commands unjust and Cruel things,
We are not to obey her.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: Oh, sits the Wind there?

speeches.speaker: Clar.
verse: Pray see what an excellent shape it has?
Why should it be infectious?

speeches.speaker: Aglau.
prose:
I have heard my Mother say, I had a Father: And was not
he a Man?

speeches.speaker: Ariad.
verse: Questionless, Madam.

speeches.speaker: Aglau.
verse: Your Fathers too, were men?

speeches.speaker: Clita.
verse: Without doubt.

speeches.speaker: Aglau.
verse: And without such, it is impossible
We cou'd have bin.

speeches.speaker: Hip.
prose: A sin against Nature, to deny it.

speeches.speaker: Aglau.
prose: Nor can we ever hope to be made Mothers without 'em.

speeches.speaker: Menal.
prose: Never, never; 'tis impossible.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
prose: Ay, by my faith is it.

speeches.speaker: Clar.
prose:
Why, how then could you have design of killing the likeness
of the thing by which you are.

speeches.speaker: Hip.
prose: Only in obedience to your Mother.

speeches.speaker: Clar.
prose:
Age is not sensible of it's own Barbarity. I swear I am resolv'd
to defend and keep him.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
prose: For your own Use.

speeches.speaker: Ariad.
prose: Nay, if you are resolv'd on't, I'le assist you.

speeches.speaker: Ariad.
prose: And I.

speeches.speaker: Menal.
prose: And I.

speeches.speaker: Clita.
prose: And all of us.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
prose:
Well, I see by instinct, though a Maid have never seen a
Man; there are some certain motions that inform her—but here's
the Protectress; now I expect a Storm.

speeches.speaker: Rosel.
verse: Child of my flesh,
But stranger to my fair unspotted mind;
Unhand this Monster.

speeches.speaker: Clar.
verse: Monster, Mother!

speeches.speaker: Rosel.
verse: Yes, Monster, I say Monster.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: Would I had him alone in my Cave for all that;
I should not be affraid he would swallow me.

speeches.speaker: Rosel.
verse: Whose every word is as a Syrens note,
To drown the careless hearer: Have I not taught the
The falsehood, and the perjuries of men?
On whom, but for a woman to shew pity,
Is to be cruel to her self: The Soveraignty,
Proud and Imperious men usurp upon us,
We confer on our selves. And love those Fetters
we fasten to our freedoms. Have we, Clarinda,
E're since Sebastian's loss, thy noble Father,
Planted our selves here in Common-VVealth,
VVith execrable Oaths, never to look
On man, but as a Monster; and wilt thou
Be the first President, to infringe those Vows
VVe made to Heaven?

speeches.speaker: Clar.
prose:
Vows made in heat, and wild temerity,
VVith Heaven, still pass for nothing. Alas! Madam, should women
always use this rigid abstinence, in a few years the whole world
would be peopled only with Beasts. Besides, pray look on him:
Is there not something nobler in his Face,
Than graces others?

speeches.speaker: Ariad.
prose:
Spoke to the purpose, Madam: Let's speak well of the man
now we have him—Come, come, there's but few of the sort.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
prose:
VVe must, and will have the man: therefore speak boldly,
Madam.

speeches.speaker: Clita
verse: Ay—or we'll shake off all Obedience.

speeches.speaker: Clar.
verse: Madam, you'l lose your Subjects hearts for ever,
If you deny this Justice.

speeches.speaker: Rosel.
verse: Are you all mad?
That no perswasion can have power upon you;
Suppose you had my Suffrage to your Suit,
Can this weak Ship-wrack'd wretch supply you all!

speeches.speaker: Hip.
verse: Not together, indeed.

speeches.speaker: Menal.
verse: No—but by Times, and Turns, he may, for ought I know.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Gracious Lady,
I have Fellows in my misery: Not far hence,
Divided only by that hellish River,
There live a Company of wretched men;
Such as your Charity may make your Slaves;
Imagine all the miseries Mankind
May suffer under: And they groan beneath 'em.

speeches.speaker: Clar.
verse: But are they all like you?

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: Speak they your Language, are they kind men?

speeches.speaker: Ariad.
verse: Are they young, healthy men? Come, there's the point.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: They were when I left 'em,
And in their May of Youth, and flowing blood,
And such as might deserve you; now cold and hunger
Hath lessen'd their perfection, but restor'd
To what they were, I doubt not they'l appear
VVorthy your favours.

speeches.speaker: Clita.
verse: This is a Blessing we could not hope for.

speeches.speaker: Clar.
verse: Dear Mother—be not obdurate.

speeches.speaker: Rosel.
verse: O thou fond foolish Girl! when thou shalt find
Their Levity, and their Neglect of Love,
Thou't mourn thy easiness, and Curse their Sex.
But come, for once your Suits are granted:
And first, all you that are for the Men, hold up your hands;
Very well.
Now you, whose colder Blood, and chaster Tempers
Bid a defiance to loves bewitching Charms,
And flight that Childish God to follow me,
Hold up your hands—is't possible, not one!

speeches.speaker: Hip.
verse: I find the Protectress will have few followers, at this rate?

speeches.speaker: Ariad.
verse: We shall have men to follow now.

speeches.speaker: Rosel.
verse: In a small Boat they shall pass over to us,
And crave comfort: If you like their Persons,
And they approve of yours; for we'll force nothing;
Each one shall choose a Husband, and enjoy
His company a Month; but that expir'd,
You shall no more come near 'em: If you prove fruitful,
The Males you shall return to them, the Females
prose:
Hear then my Resolution; and endeavour not to add to
what I grant, for 'twill be fruitless: you shall appear as good Angels
to these wretched men.

We will reserve our selves: This is the utmost you shall obtain,
Therefore as you think fit, dismiss this Stranger. And all prepare to
morrow for the meeting.

speeches.speaker: Clar.
verse: Come, Sir, pray walk with us,
prose:
We'll shew you the pleasant Groves and Springs, and Grotto's,
and you shall eat and drink with us.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Excellent Lady!
Tho' 'twill appear a Wonder, one near starv'd
Shou'd refuse Rest and Meat—I must not take
Your Noble Offer—I left in yonder Desart,
A Virgin almost pin'd.

speeches.speaker: Clar.
verse: She's not your Wife, I hope.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: No Madam—she's my Sister. 'Tis now dangerous
To speak truth—
To her I deeply vou'd not to taste Food or Rest,
Till I return'd: Now, if you please
To afford me but an easie passage thither,
And some Convenient Sustenance for her;
I shall for ever bless you, and thankfully
She shall acknowledge to you she owes her life.

speeches.speaker: Clar.
verse: You plead so well, I can deny you nothing.
Come in; and I my self will see you furnish'd,
And with the next Sun visit and relieve you.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Let this declare my thanks.

speeches.speaker: Clar.
verse: This act would prove,
In others gratitude: But in me, 'tis Love.

speeches.speaker: Frug.
prose:
OH what a Tempest have I in my Stomach?
My Guts are grumbling a kind of Tune,
Like the Base Pipes of an Organ: I am starv'd into a Substance so
thin, that my Body is transparent; you may see my heart, and the
appurtenances, hang up here in its mortal Closet, as easily as a Candle
in a Lanthorn.

speeches.speaker: Haz.
prose: For my part, I've forgot to eat.

My Bellies grown together, like an empty Satchel. I have bin throwing
a main yonder, to pass away the time: But I can get nothing—my
Guts grumble still.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose: I am thinking, Gentlemen, what a happiness—

speeches.speaker: Hazard.
prose:
How's that! have you the Courage to think of any happiness!
Gad you have a hoard of meat then, Sirrah. You could never
have a happy thought, without the encouragement of Beef, or some
such Blessing.

speeches.speaker: Frug.
prose:
Beef, Rogues, Beef; who the Devil talks of Beef there?




I'le draw. I rage, I storm lowder than the Winds or Weather.
I am not naturally Valliant, but to provoke my Courage with the
sound of Beef, and give me none, makes me a fury—I roar like
the Sea: Therefore you happy Rascal, make attonement quickly;
or in the name of Famin, I will so grind you—ah—

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose:
Is the Devil in you? Why I am more starv'd than any of
ye, have three times louder Bag-pipes in my Guts. And am ten
times as thin, I was diving in the Sea to find Oysters last night, and
the Saylers took me for Will with the Wisp—The Moon shone
quite through me.

speeches.speaker: Surg.
prose:
Why, Sirrah, what happiness is that you are thinking of then?
Answer me that.

speeches.speaker: Frug.
prose:
Ay, ay, answer that; the Dog has blood in's face; an apparent
sign of nourishment, he has Eaten lately—I fee't plainly—this
Rogue has half an Ox by him, I warrant, in some corner now—hah—my
Mouth Waters at the Rascal Confoundedly.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose:
An Ox! Oh Parradise! 'Sbud, wou'd I had but the Hoof of
one, on Condition you were all hang'd—or any part else that
had the honour of belonging to blessed Beef.

speeches.speaker: Frug.
prose:
Pox on thee, do not talk on't then: Do not charm my starving
Intellects, with that most delightful sound—Now if I were
a great man, the word should be nothing but Beef, through my Kingdome;
my Armies should exercise nothing else: And my Butcher
should mouth it instead of a Drum.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose:
When I was speaking of happiness: I was thinking what a
pleasure my Dogs had, when I kept House at Home—they had a
Store-House, a Store-House of most blessed Bones, and Crusts; hard
and happy Crusts.

speeches.speaker: Haz.
prose:
Would I had one to gnaw now: or were but amongst 'em;
I'd snarl for a short Dinner with 'em.

speeches.speaker: Frug.
prose:
Now has this tantalizing Rogue set my Mouth a watering,
a second time, with talking of his Hounds.

speeches.speaker: Haz.
prose:
A Son of a Whore, when he knows too, that a fat Beagle is
as good as a fat Buck—And that the Loyn of a Bull-dog—

speeches.speaker: Frug.
prose: Ah, is better than a Loyn of Veal a thousand times.

speeches.speaker: Surg.
verse: Here comes the Woman;
It may be she has meat, and may relieve us,
Let's stand aside and mark, and then be ready—she'll hide her
Store else, and so Cozen us.

speeches.speaker: Amint.
verse: How weary, and how faint is all my Body,
My Eyes like spent Lamps, going out, grow
Heavy; my sight forsaking me, and all my Spirits,
As if they heard my passing Bell toll for me,
Take in their Powers, and leave me up to Destiny,
Oh for a little meat! a little water.
I had whole Floods of Tears awhile, that nourisht me,
But they are all consum'd for thee, Marine;
For thou art dead. Oh take my life, sweet Heav'n!
Or make me once more happy in his sight.

speeches.speaker: Frug.
verse: She's faln asleep, sure?
Why should she have this Blessing, and we wake?

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose:
This thing has bin our ruine: The Captain had not gone
to Sea, but for her sake; and all those mischiefs that are fallen upon
us, are come by her means.

speeches.speaker: Frug.
prose:
Why should we consume thus and starve? Have nothing to
relieve us: And she live there that bred our Miseries, unrosted or
unboil'd, hah!

speeches.speaker: Haz.
prose:
Right; I have read in Histories of such restoring Meats:
Besides, we have Examples, a thousand Examples, Women that have
eaten their Children, Men their Slaves, nay, their Brothers: But
these are nothing; Husbands devour'd their Wives. (They are their
Chattels.) And of a School-master, that, in time of Famin, powdred
up all his Scholars—she's young and tidy—on my Conscience
she'll eat delicately, just like young Pork; a little leaner: your
Opinion, Surgeon?

speeches.speaker: Surg.
prose: I think she may be good meat; but we shall want Salt.

speeches.speaker: Frug.
prose: A pox, she wants no powdring, Man.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose:
But to suck out the humorous parts: by all means let's kill
her in a Chafe; she'll eat the sweeter.

speeches.speaker: Surg.
prose:
Let's kill her any way, and kill her quickly; that we may
go to supper.

speeches.speaker: Haz.
prose: But how if the Captain—

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose: Oh—he's dead, and the rest famish'd. Come, wake her,

speeches.speaker: Surgeon.
prose: Cut her throat, and then divide her; Every man his share.

speeches.speaker: Haz.
prose: Hush—she wakes her self—

speeches.speaker: Amint.
prose:
Who's there! Oh, Gentlemen! give me some Food, or else
I perish: I am just now dying.

speeches.speaker: Surg.
verse: You'l save a labour then: You bred our miseries,
And you shall pay for't: We have no meat;
But all are sick and famisht: However, e're
We dye, we'll have one dainty meal.

speeches.speaker: Amint.
verse: Shall I be with you, Gentlemen?

speeches.speaker: Frug.
verse: Yes, marry shall you; in our Bellies, sweet Lady:
You see we love you well.

speeches.speaker: Amint.
verse: What said you, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Frug.
verse: Why, Faith, only we'll eat your Ladiship, that's all.

speeches.speaker: Surg.
verse: Come, come: Say your prayers, that I may perform—
We are wondrous sharp set. Come, Gentlemen.
Who are for the ^ parts?

speeches.speaker: Fran.
verse: I, I.

speeches.speaker: Frug.
verse: I, I.

speeches.speaker: Surg.
verse: Pray be patient: They will not fall to every ones share.

speeches.speaker: Amint.
verse: Oh, hear me! hear me, you barbarous Men!

speeches.speaker: Surg.
verse: Not a word—

speeches.speaker: D. Pier.
verse: The Lady's Voice! stand off, Slaves! How now,
What d'ee intend, Villains?

speeches.speaker: Amint.
verse: Oh, my dear Friend!

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: My kindest, best Aminta! see, what I have brought thee?

speeches.speaker: Bolds.
verse: —These Rogues would have ravish'd her.
Speak, how was it, Lady?

speeches.speaker: Amint.
verse: Forgive 'em, 'Twas their hungers.

speeches.speaker: D. Pier.
verse: Their Hungers! Choak 'em, they would have eaten her!
Oh damn'd Canibals! speak, is it true?

speeches.speaker: Frug.
verse: For my part, I confess an appetite.

speeches.speaker: D. Pier.
prose:
An appetite! I'll fit you for your appetite! since you
would be such Devils! why did you not begin with one another
handsomely? And spare the Woman to beget more Food on?

speeches.speaker: Amint.
prose:
For my sake spare 'em, Lieutenant: And pray come into
the Cave, and eat with us.

speeches.speaker: D. Pier.
prose: Stir not within forty foot of this Food, if you do, Dogs—

speeches.speaker: Omnes.
prose: Oh Lieutenant! Lieutenant! Dear noble Lieutenant.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: And with Devotion thank the Powr's above,
For giving me this means to serve my Love.
prose:
Come Master, and honest Sailers: Let's go in:
Oh my Dear! I have strange news to tell thee: I have discover'd a
new World, a Paradise of Angels, such as thou art; that have supply'd
me with these Meats and Drinks. We shall see 'em to morrow,
and they'l relieve us further: I'le tell thee more within.

speeches.speaker: Amint.
verse: Thou best of men! how am I bound to thee.

speeches.speaker: La Mur.
prose:
FInd d'em out quickly, vid out excuse or delays, or begar
your Troate sal be Cut.

speeches.speaker: Sebast.
prose:
Alas, Sir, we left 'em here: But you see the place is fatal,
and who knows but they may be starv'd, and dead, and rotten.

speeches.speaker: La Mur.
prose:
Rotten: De Dev'la rot 'em! dat is no matre, I vil have
my revenge on d'em; dead or alive! Morbleu! I vil search every
Corner of de World, but I vill have d'em.

speeches.speaker: Nicus.
prose:
You see these Foot-steps, and the tracks new made, shew that
they have bin here—hah! and see a further discovery—what's
that moves there upon the River?

speeches.speaker: Bourc.
prose:
I see it now plainly. 'Tis a Vessel, and throng'd with
people—They seem as sailing over to that other Country
there.

speeches.speaker: Sebast.
prose:
'Tis they, Sir. I know the Captain by his Feather; and if
you observe narrowly, look yonder, you may see the Woman too.

speeches.speaker: La Mur.
prose: Oh Diable! it is she, begar I know her.

speeches.speaker: Bour.
prose: But how is't possible they should get thither?

speeches.speaker: Sebast.
prose:
That indeed is most difficult: And much I wonder by
what strange adventure they had this help: Yet thus far I can advise
you, whil'st we were Crusing up and down, before you took us,
we chanc'd to touch upon a place, govern'd by Women, and went
by night on shore to get fresh Water: Thither, as I suppose, that
Vessel's gone; for it lies Westward.

speeches.speaker: La Mur.
prose:
Shew us de vay, make us come thither, or begar you
sal be no living Creature.

speeches.speaker: Sebast.
prose: Sir, I'le do the best I can, tho' I am but an ill Pilot.

speeches.speaker: La Mur.
prose: Look to't: For if you fail, expect no mercy.

speeches.speaker: Nicus.
prose: Was ever Fate like ours, to be so taken.

speeches.speaker: Sebast.
prose:
And by this Vallain La Mure too! for now I know
'Tis hee, tho' misery and Age disguise me from him.
But to relieve us—take this advise, Son, when we are landed
yonder, instead of searching for the Fugitive Woman, throw thy
self on the mercy of the Protectress; there's more pity to be expected
from them, than from this Barb'rous Wretch.

speeches.speaker: Nicus.
prose:
Well counsell'd, Sir—I'le do't—and hope good Heaven




will take compassion on us.

speeches.speaker: Sebast.
prose: We are undone else.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
prose:
Come, my dear, the Song, the Song! methinks I'm so merry
o'th' suddain!

A SONG.

CInthia, with an awful Power,
O're all Hearts extends her sway:
Did the Eastern Natives know her,
They'd less prize the God of Day.
On her Brow Night shady lyes,
Whilst Morning Breaks from her fair Eyes.


2.
When she Dances, all the Graces
Charming motion treat your Eyes;
When she sings, she doubly blesses,
With her skill, and Angels Voice.
Musicks soul in Airs sublime,
Whilst every Heart still beats the time.


3.
When she smiles, you may discover
Golden Coasts, and wealthy Bliss;
But her Frowns throw back each Lover.

To Cold Green-land, where we freeze.
Men may see the Glittering Shore,
But ne're deserve, to reach the Ore.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
prose:
This is the happiest Day that ever blest our Life.
Some of the men are landed already.

speeches.speaker: Hip.
prose: Where, where! did you see 'em, my Dear?

speeches.speaker: Iul.
prose:
Through the West-Gate of the Garden that looks towards
the Sea. Well, I swear there's one of 'em so pretty a fellow, that
I could not forbear Oagling him for my Heart.

speeches.speaker: Ariad.
prose:
You mad Creature, you: And yet he may be a Monster
under his Clothes, for ought you know.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
prose:
If he were: He is not the first Monster a Woman has bin
fond of, I hope. I knew one so fond of a Monkey once, she desir'd
to be marry'd to't.

speeches.speaker: Menal.
prose:
Why really the Masculine Creature comes so near the Nature
of Humanity, that really one would wonder: But did she desire
to wed the Creature!

speeches.speaker: Hip.
prose:
But, Sister, prithee are they all young Men: Can'st thou tell?
For you know Age will but trouble us; Their Imperfections are
not to be reform'd: And your man, when he comes to be old, is
good for little or nothing.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
prose:
Why, troth, I think these are a mixt Party, some young,
some old; some weak, and some strong; some that look briskly,
as if they had Wit; and others Clownishly, as if they might
be made Fools.

speeches.speaker: Hip.
prose:
Venus direct me to one of them. I long to make a Fool of
a Man strangely.

speeches.speaker: Clita.
prose:
Ay, that's a general longing amongst us: For I never
